props.title: The St. Valentine's Day Massacre

sections.content: Roger Corman's The St. Valentine's Day Massacre (1967) stands as a brutal, documentary-style recreation of Chicago's most infamous gangland killing. Unlike the romanticized gangster films of the 1930s like Little Caesar (1931) and The Public Enemy (1931), Corman's film takes a cold, almost clinical approach to mob violence. Jason Robards delivers a fierce performance as Al Capone, though he was notably older than the real-life Capone was during these events. The film's quasi-documentary style, complete with authoritative narration, influenced later crime films like Goodfellas (1990) and Casino (1995). The St. Valentine's Day Massacre|1967|Roger Corman's detailed recreation of the 1929 Chicago mob killings with Jason Robards as Al Capone|Prime Video Scarface|1932|The original gangster classic loosely based on Al Capone's rise to power|TCM The Untouchables|1987|Brian De Palma's stylish take on Eliot Ness's war against Capone with Robert De Niro and Kevin Costner|Paramount+

The film marked a significant departure for Roger Corman, known primarily for his low-budget horror films like House of Usher (1960) and The Pit and the Pendulum (1961). With The St. Valentine's Day Massacre, Corman secured his largest budget to date ($1 million from 20th Century Fox) and delivered a methodical chronicle of mob warfare. The film's influence can be seen in later historical crime dramas like Once Upon a Time in America (1984) and Miller's Crossing (1990), which similarly attempted to deglamorize gangster violence while maintaining historical accuracy.

What sets this film apart is its attention to period detail and historical accuracy. Unlike more sensationalized gangster pictures like Dillinger (1973) or Baby Face Nelson (1957), Corman's film maintains a commitment to documenting the actual events leading up to the massacre. The production design by Daniel Haller meticulously recreates 1929 Chicago, while the use of newspaper headlines and radio reports grounds the narrative in historical reality. Road to Perdition|2002|Depression-era gangster drama about a mob enforcer protecting his son|Netflix Capone|2020|Tom Hardy stars as an aging Al Capone dealing with dementia|Prime Video Miller's Crossing|1990|Coen Brothers' stylish take on Prohibition-era gang warfare|Hulu SUBHEAD: Impact on Crime Cinema

The film's documentary approach influenced a wave of true-crime gangster films that followed, including Bonnie and Clyde (1967) and Dillinger (1973). Its unflinching portrayal of violence, while tame by today's standards, pushed boundaries for 1967 and helped pave the way for the more graphic gangster films of the 1970s like The Godfather (1972) and Mean Streets (1973).
